objective_pt: Challenge an argument, rebut a point and defend your position politely but firmly ("That's a fair point, but...", "I'd take issue with...", "The evidence suggests otherwise").

teacher.goal_pt: Get the learner arguing about a light topic and notice how they disagree.
prompts: Pineapple on pizza: yes or no? Convince me.
What's the strongest argument against your view?
watchFor: "I don't agree with you" as the only option; introduce "I see it differently".
"I agree with you" pronounced as "I am agree" (from "eu concordo").

exercises.prompt: That's a fair point, but I see it differently.
accepted: That's a fair point, but I see it differently
That is a fair point but I see it differently

exercises.instruction_pt: Which is the most natural way to disagree in a formal debate?
options: I am not agree with this.
With all due respect, I'd take issue with that claim.
exercises.explanation_pt: "With all due respect" plus "take issue with" is firm but polite. "I am not agree" is a typical Brazilian error: "agree" is a verb, so "I don't agree".

exercises.instruction_pt: Say this in natural English: "Eu discordo totalmente."
accepted: I totally disagree
I completely disagree
I strongly disagree
I disagree completely
I disagree entirely
I couldn't disagree more
I entirely disagree
I fully disagree

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "Agree" and "disagree" are verbs, so don't use "am": "I disagree", not "I am disagree".
commonErrors.correction_en: I totally disagree.

teacher.goal_pt: Language for rebuttal: take issue with, concede, counterargument, hold water, the burden of proof.
prompts: Which popular belief do you think doesn't hold water?
Can you concede one point to someone you disagree with?
watchFor: "Argument" used to mean "discussion" only; in English it can also mean a fight.
"Discuss about" (from "discutir sobre"); "discuss" takes a direct object.

exercises.example_en: I'd take issue with the idea that money buys happiness.
That theory doesn't really hold water.

exercises.meaning_pt: admitir, reconhecer (um ponto do outro lado)
exercises.example_en: I'll concede that the costs are high.

exercises.instruction_pt: Match each debating expression with its meaning.
Say this in natural English: "Vamos discutir esse ponto."
accepted: Let's discuss this point
Let's discuss that point
Let's talk about this point
Let's talk about that point
Let's go over this point
Let's look at this point
Let's discuss this

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "Discuss" takes a direct object: "discuss this point", never "discuss about". ("Talk about" does take "about".)
commonErrors.correction_en: Let's discuss this point.

teacher.goal_pt: Use contrastive stress to highlight the point you are challenging.
prompts: Say "I didn't say it was EASY, I said it was POSSIBLE."
Which word would you stress to challenge the number in "Most people agree"?
watchFor: Even stress on every word, so the contrast disappears.
Adding a vowel to final consonants: "issue-e", "point-chi".

exercises.instruction_pt: Repeat, stressing "cause" and "symptom" to contrast them.
exercises.prompt: That's not the cause, it's a symptom.
accepted: That's not the cause, it's a symptom
That is not the cause, it is a symptom

exercises.instruction_pt: Repeat. "Doesn't" is stressed; "hold water" links smoothly.
exercises.prompt: With respect, that argument doesn't hold water.
accepted: With respect, that argument doesn't hold water
With respect, that argument does not hold water

exercises.instruction_pt: In "I said SOME people, not ALL people", why are "some" and "all" stressed?
options: Because they are at the start of a phrase.
exercises.explanation_pt: English uses stress to mark contrast. Stressing the words you are correcting makes your rebuttal clear.

teacher.goal_pt: Follow the structure of an argument (claim, concession, rebuttal) and respond to it.
prompts: What was their main point after "but"?
watchFor: Focusing on the concession and missing the real point after "but" or "however".
Replying "I agree" without saying with what.

exercises.instruction_pt: Listen. What is the speaker's main point?
exercises.listen: Admittedly, public transport is expensive to build. But in the long run, it saves cities far more than it costs.
options: Public transport pays off over time.
Cities should stop building public transport.
exercises.explanation_pt: "Admittedly" introduces a concession; the main point comes after "But": it saves more than it costs.

exercises.instruction_pt: Listen and rebut the claim politely: make a concession, then say it has also done a lot of good.
exercises.listen: Social media has done more harm than good.
accepted: That's a fair point, but it has also done a lot of good
I see your point, but it has also done a lot of good
That may be true, but it has also done a lot of good
That's true to some extent, but it has also done a lot of good
I take your point, but it has also done a lot of good
You have a point, but it has also done a lot of good
Fair point, but it has also done a lot of good
I see what you mean, but it has also done a lot of good
Maybe, but it has also done a lot of good
*, but it has also done a lot of good
*, but it's also done a lot of good

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "Você tem razão" is "You're right" or "You have a point", not "you have reason".
commonErrors.correction_en: You have a point, but it has also done a lot of good.

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "Agree" is a verb: "I agree" / "I don't agree".
commonErrors.correction_en: I don't entirely agree. It has also done a lot of good.

exercises.instruction_pt: Listen and ask the speaker to back up their claim.
exercises.listen: Everyone knows that young people don't read anymore.
accepted: What evidence do you have for that?
Where's the evidence for that?
Is there any evidence for that?
What makes you say that?
What's that based on?
Do you have any data to back that up?
Can you back that up?
How do you know that?
What's your evidence?
Says who?

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "Evidence" is uncountable in English: "some evidence", "any evidence", never "evidences".
commonErrors.correction_en: What evidence do you have for that?

commonErrors.explanation_pt: The noun is "proof" (uncountable) or "evidence"; "proves" is a verb form.
commonErrors.correction_en: What evidence do you have for that?

teacher.goal_pt: Run a short structured debate: claim, support, concession, rebuttal, conclusion.
prompts: Should university be free for everyone?
I'll play devil's advocate. What would you say to someone who says it's too expensive?
Can you sum up your position in one sentence?
watchFor: Personal attacks or overly direct language ("You're wrong").

exercises.instruction_pt: Say this in natural English: "Concordo em parte, mas acho que você está ignorando os custos."
accepted: I partly agree, but I think you're ignoring the costs
I agree up to a point, but I think you're ignoring the costs
I agree to some extent, but I think you're ignoring the costs
I partially agree, but I think you're ignoring the costs
I partly agree, but I think you're overlooking the costs
I agree in part, but I think you're ignoring the costs
I agree with you in part, but I think you're overlooking the costs

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "Agree" is a verb: "I partly agree", not "I am partly agree".
commonErrors.correction_en: I partly agree, but I think you're ignoring the costs.

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "Em parte" is "in part" or "partly" (singular), not "in parts".
commonErrors.correction_en: I partly agree, but I think you're ignoring the costs.

exercises.instruction_pt: Say this in natural English: "Só para bancar o advogado do diabo: e se isso não funcionar?"
accepted: Just to play devil's advocate, what if it doesn't work?
Just to play devil's advocate, what if this doesn't work?
Just to play devil's advocate, what if that doesn't work?
To play devil's advocate, what if it doesn't work?
Playing devil's advocate, what if it doesn't work?
Let me play devil's advocate. What if it doesn't work?

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "E se...?" is "What if...?" in English. "And if..." sounds incomplete.
commonErrors.correction_en: Just to play devil's advocate, what if it doesn't work?

commonErrors.explanation_pt: The fixed expression is "devil's advocate", not "devil's lawyer".
commonErrors.correction_en: Just to play devil's advocate, what if it doesn't work?

exercises.instruction_pt: Role-play: challenge your friend's view and propose an alternative.
exercises.scene_pt: A friend has strong views about phones in schools.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.text: Phones should be banned in schools, full stop.

turns.speaker: you
turns.cue_pt: Say you'd take issue with that, at least for older students.
accepted: I'd take issue with that, at least for older students
I'd take issue with that, at least when it comes to older students
I'd disagree with that, at least for older students
I'd take issue with that, at least for older kids
I'm not sure I agree, at least for older students
I'd question that, at least for older students

commonErrors.explanation_pt: The expression is "take issue with".
commonErrors.correction_en: I'd take issue with that.

turns.speaker: you
turns.cue_pt: Say they can be, but they're also a useful learning tool.
accepted: They can be, but they're also a useful learning tool
They can be, but they're also a useful tool for learning
They can be a distraction, but they're also a useful learning tool
Sometimes, but they're also a useful learning tool
They can be, but they can also be a useful learning tool
True, but they're also a useful learning tool

commonErrors.explanation_pt: After "for" use -ing: "a tool for learning".
commonErrors.correction_en: They're also a useful tool for learning.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.text: Fine, I'll concede that. But who's going to control how they use them?

turns.speaker: you
turns.cue_pt: Say teachers could set clear rules, rather than ban them outright.
accepted: Teachers could set clear rules, rather than ban them outright
Teachers could set clear rules rather than banning them outright
Teachers could set clear rules instead of banning them outright
Teachers could set clear rules instead of banning them completely
Teachers could just set clear rules rather than ban them outright
Schools could set clear rules rather than ban them outright

commonErrors.explanation_pt: After "instead of" use -ing: "instead of banning".
commonErrors.correction_en: Instead of banning them outright.

exercises.instruction_pt: Respond to the claim in about a minute, as if in a debate.
exercises.prompt_en: Here's my position: university education should be completely free for everyone. Convince me I'm wrong, or tell me why I'm right.
guidelines_pt: State your position clearly in the first sentence.
Concede one point: "I'll grant you that...".
Rebut with a reason and, if possible, evidence.

teacher.goal_pt: Recycle rebuttal language and the key grammar traps (agree, discuss, evidence).
prompts: Disagree with me politely: "Cats are better than dogs."

exercises.instruction_pt: Say this in natural English: "Esse argumento não se sustenta."
accepted: That argument doesn't hold water
This argument doesn't hold water
That argument doesn't stand up
That argument doesn't hold up
This argument doesn't hold up
That argument doesn't stand up to scrutiny
That argument is not convincing

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "Sustentar-se" (an argument) is "hold water" or "hold up". "Sustain itself" is a literal translation.
commonErrors.correction_en: That argument doesn't hold water.

exercises.sentence: There isn't enough ___ to support that claim.
accepted: evidence
proof
data

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "Evidence" and "proof" are uncountable here: no plural.
commonErrors.correction_en: There isn't enough evidence to support that claim.

options: I admit you're right about that.
exercises.explanation_pt: "I'll grant you that" is a concession: you admit the other person has a point.

exercises.prompt: All things considered, I stand by what I said.
accepted: All things considered, I stand by what I said

practice.example_en: She calmly rebutted every point he made.

practice.meaning_pt: espantalho: uma versão distorcida do argumento do outro
practice.example_en: That's a straw man. I never said we should cut all funding.
Can you back that up with any data?
She made a compelling case for changing the policy.

practice.instruction_pt: Repeat with natural rhythm and stress.
practice.prompt: I take your point, but the figures tell a different story.
accepted: I take your point, but the figures tell a different story
I take your point, but the figures tell another story

practice.instruction_pt: Repeat with natural rhythm and stress.
practice.prompt: That's a bit of a sweeping generalisation.
accepted: That's a bit of a sweeping generalisation
That's a bit of a sweeping generalization
That is a bit of a sweeping generalisation

practice.instruction_pt: Repeat with natural rhythm and stress.
practice.prompt: Where's the evidence to back that up?
accepted: Where's the evidence to back that up
Where is the evidence to back that up

practice.instruction_pt: Repeat in a calm, firm tone.
practice.prompt: Let me finish my point, if I may.
accepted: Let me finish my point, if I may
Let me just finish my point, if I may

practice.instruction_pt: Repeat with natural rhythm and stress.
practice.prompt: I'm afraid I can't agree with you on that one.
accepted: I'm afraid I can't agree with you on that one
I'm afraid I can't agree with you on that
I am afraid I cannot agree with you on that one

practice.instruction_pt: Say this in natural English: "Você tem um ponto, mas isso não prova nada."
accepted: You have a point, but that doesn't prove anything
You've got a point, but that doesn't prove anything
You have a point, but it doesn't prove anything
That's a fair point, but it doesn't prove anything
Fair point, but that doesn't prove anything
You have a point, but that proves nothing
You've got a point, but it doesn't prove anything
I take your point, but that doesn't prove anything

commonErrors.explanation_pt: English avoids double negatives: "doesn't prove anything" or "proves nothing".
commonErrors.correction_en: That doesn't prove anything.

practice.instruction_pt: Say this in natural English: "Isso é exatamente o que eu quero dizer."
accepted: That's exactly what I mean
That's exactly my point
That is exactly what I mean
That's exactly what I'm saying
That's exactly what I'm trying to say
Exactly my point
That's precisely my point
That's precisely what I mean

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "Quero dizer" here means "I mean", not "I want to say".
commonErrors.correction_en: That's exactly what I mean.

practice.instruction_pt: Say this in natural English: "Com todo o respeito, os números não confirmam isso."
accepted: With all due respect, the numbers don't support that
With all due respect, the figures don't support that
With respect, the numbers don't back that up
With all due respect, the numbers don't back that up
With all due respect, the figures don't back that up
With all due respect, the numbers don't confirm that
With respect, the figures don't support that
With all due respect, the data doesn't support that
With all due respect, the data don't support that

commonErrors.explanation_pt: The fixed phrase is "with all due respect" or simply "with respect".
commonErrors.correction_en: With all due respect, the numbers don't support that.

practice.instruction_pt: Say this in natural English: "Eu admito que você tem razão nesse ponto."
accepted: I admit you're right on that point
I admit that you're right on that point
I'll admit you're right on that point
I concede you're right on that point
I'll concede that point
I concede that point
I'll grant you that
I'll give you that
Okay, you're right on that point
I admit you're right about that

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "Ter razão" is "to be right", not "to have reason".
commonErrors.correction_en: I admit you're right on that point.

practice.instruction_pt: Say this in natural English: "Isso não tem nada a ver com o que estamos discutindo."
accepted: That has nothing to do with what we're discussing
That's got nothing to do with what we're discussing
That has nothing to do with what we're talking about
That's nothing to do with what we're discussing
That has nothing to do with the issue we're discussing
That's irrelevant to what we're discussing
That has nothing to do with what we are discussing

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "Não tem nada a ver" is "has nothing to do with".
commonErrors.correction_en: That has nothing to do with what we're discussing.

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "Discuss" takes a direct object: "discuss something", not "discuss about".
commonErrors.correction_en: What we're discussing.

practice.instruction_pt: Listen and politely challenge the idea that it's the only solution.
practice.listen: Surely a ban on cars in the city centre is the only solution?
accepted: Not necessarily
I'm not sure it's the only solution
I wouldn't say it's the only solution

I'm not convinced it's the only solution

Not necessarily. Better public transport could help too

commonErrors.explanation_pt: The adverb is "not necessarily".
commonErrors.correction_en: Not necessarily.

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "A única solução" is "the only solution". "Unique" means "one of a kind".
commonErrors.correction_en: It's not the only solution.

practice.instruction_pt: Listen and give a qualified answer: partly agree, but say qualifications matter too.
practice.listen: But don't you agree that experience matters more than qualifications?
accepted: Up to a point, but qualifications matter too

Both matter, I'd say
I'd say both matter
*, but qualifications matter too
*, but qualifications still matter

commonErrors.explanation_pt: The preposition is "to": "to some extent".

practice.instruction_pt: Listen and answer: say yes and point to a source.
practice.listen: Can you back that up with any evidence?
accepted: Yes, there's a recent study that shows it
Yes, a recent study backs it up
Yes, there's a study that backs it up
Yes, the latest report backs it up

Yes, * backs it up

Yes, there's a * that shows it
Yes, the * back it up
Sure, * backs it up

commonErrors.explanation_pt: "Research" is uncountable: say "some research", "a study" or "a piece of research".
commonErrors.correction_en: There's a recent study that shows it.

practice.instruction_pt: Argue a position for about a minute, then rebut one objection.
practice.prompt_en: Should university education be free for everyone?
guidelines_pt: State your position clearly in the first sentence.
Back it up with one reason and one example.
Raise an objection yourself: "Some would argue that..." and rebut it.

practice.instruction_pt: Role-play: disagree with your manager politely but firmly.
practice.scene_pt: Your manager wants to move the office out of the city. You see problems with the idea.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.text: I think moving the office out of the city is the obvious choice. The rent is half the price.

turns.speaker: you
turns.cue_pt: Acknowledge the point, but say you see it differently.
accepted: I take your point, but I see it differently
Fair point, but I see things differently
I see what you mean, but I see it differently
That's true, but I see it a bit differently
I take your point, but I don't quite see it that way
I hear you, but I see it differently

commonErrors.explanation_pt: Use the adverb: "I see it differently".
commonErrors.correction_en: I see it differently.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.text: Go on, then. What's the problem?

turns.speaker: you
turns.cue_pt: Say the commute would be much longer for most of the team.
accepted: The commute would be much longer for most of the team
The commute would be a lot longer for most of the team
Most of the team would have a much longer commute
For most of the team, the commute would be much longer
Most of us would have a much longer commute
It would mean a much longer commute for most of the team

commonErrors.explanation_pt: Short adjectives take -er: "longer", not "more long".
commonErrors.correction_en: A much longer commute.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.text: People can work from home a couple of days a week. It evens out.

turns.speaker: you
turns.cue_pt: Say that argument doesn't quite hold water, because some roles need people on site.
accepted: That argument doesn't quite hold water, because some roles need people on site
I don't think that quite holds water, because some roles need people on site
That doesn't quite hold water, because some roles need people on site
That argument doesn't really hold water, since some roles need people on site
That doesn't really hold water, because some jobs need people on site
I'm not sure that holds water, because some roles need people on site

commonErrors.explanation_pt: The idiom is "hold water", with no article.
commonErrors.correction_en: That argument doesn't hold water.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.text: Hmm. So where does that leave us?

turns.speaker: you
turns.cue_pt: Suggest looking at the figures in more detail before deciding.
accepted: Let's look at the figures in more detail before we decide
Let's look at the figures in more detail before deciding

practice.instruction_pt: Which phrase introduces a counterargument?
practice.explanation_pt: "Having said that" signals a contrast with what came before. The others add more of the same.

practice.instruction_pt: What is a "straw man" argument?
options: Misrepresenting someone's view so it's easier to attack
An argument based only on statistics
practice.explanation_pt: A straw man distorts the other side's position and then attacks the distorted version.

practice.instruction_pt: Listen. What does the speaker do?
practice.listen: I'll grant you that the costs are high, but the long-term benefits far outweigh them.
options: She rejects the point about costs.
She concedes a point, then defends her position.
practice.explanation_pt: "I'll grant you that..." concedes; "but the benefits far outweigh them" defends her view.

on
upon

accepted: with
